title.title: The crossing number of $K_n$ is $Z(n)$
title.subtitle: Claim: the Harary–Hill formula holds for every $n$, and Zarankiewicz's for every $K_{m,n}$

object.heading: $K_7$ on two pages: vertices on a line, every edge above or below it

beats.text: Edge $ij$ goes above when $(i+j) \bmod 7 < 3$, below otherwise
This drawing has $Z(7) = 9$ crossings. The claim: no drawing has fewer

achievement.label: Conjectures of Guy, Harary–Hill (1960s) and Zarankiewicz (1954)
achievement.context: Before: exact only up to $n = 14$; the best general lower bound was about 98.56% of $Z(n)$

verify.detail: Both formulas, over arbitrary continuous drawings, in about 18k and 21k lines of Lean
verify.ourCheck: We read the Lean statements line by line; we did not build them

sources.quote: For every n >= 3, cr(K_n) = (1/4) floor(n/2) floor((n-1)/2) floor((n-2)/2) floor((n-3)/2) (Harary–Hill/Guy conjecture), and for all positive m,n, cr(K_{m,n}) = floor(m/2) floor((m-1)/2) floor(n/2) floor((n-1)/2) (Zarankiewicz conjecture
Harary–Hill (1963) and Guy (1960) for K_n; known exactly up to n=12 (Pan–Richter 2007) and n=14 (Aichholzer 2021, computer-assisted); asymptotic ratio > 0.98559895

plain: Draw every pair of dots joined by a line; how few crossings can you get away with?

steps: Turn any drawing into a list of polynomials
Each polynomial claims its own pair of crossing lines
So a drawing needs at least as many crossings as the formula

data.label: one-to-one: crossings at least the count

voice.text: Seven dots, every pair joined. This drawing has nine crossings, exactly the formula.
The proof turns any drawing into polynomials, each claiming its own crossing pair.
